summary: A film of awe, curiosity, and distrust, in which apes and astronauts meet the monolith and a calm machine turns on the men who doubt it.

need-to-breathe.why: Bowman blows the pod's bolts and crosses the vacuum to the airlock without a helmet, Poole's air hose is severed, and the hibernating crew's life functions flatline.

hungry.why: The apes grub for roots and lose the waterhole until the bone lets them eat tapir, and the astronauts suck liquid meals through straws.

thirsty.why: In the Dawn of Man the tribes squabble over the one waterhole in a parched landscape.

need-to-poop.why: Floyd studies the ten-point instructions for the zero-gravity toilet aboard the shuttle.

need-to-pee.why: The zero-gravity toilet instructions cover this too; Floyd reads them at length.

sleepy.why: Floyd dozes on the shuttle with his pen floating free, three crew sleep in hibernation, and Poole lies under a sunlamp while the ship runs itself.

dizzy.why: The spinning space station and Discovery's centrifuge, and the Star Gate's roaring tunnel of light that leaves Bowman shuddering, make vertigo part of the film's physics.

fatigued.why: Poole jogs the centrifuge and Bowman labors in the pod, but exertion is slight.

pain.why: A leopard takes one of the apes, Moon-Watcher clubs the rival ape to death with a bone, and Poole is sent tumbling, hose cut, into space.

disgusted.why: Nothing disgusts anyone; even the apes' raw tapir meat is eaten with relish.

over-stimulated.why: The monolith at Tycho emits a shriek that doubles the astronauts over clutching their helmets, and the Star Gate assaults Bowman with light and color.

too-hot-too-cold.why: The apes live in a sun-baked, drought-stricken landscape, and the cold vacuum takes Poole.

afraid.why: The apes cower from the leopard and the monolith, Bowman is locked out by HAL and told the conversation can serve no purpose, and HAL himself says he is afraid as his mind goes.

anxious.why: Poole and Bowman retreat to the pod to discuss whether to disconnect HAL, and HAL probes Bowman about his doubts over the mission's strange rumors.

panic.why: The apes scatter in panic when the leopard strikes, and Bowman races out in the pod after Poole's tumbling body.

sensory-pleasures.why: The apes gorge on tapir meat, Poole basks under the sunlamp, and the aged Bowman dines alone in the white room, but pleasure is faint.

aesthetic-pleasures.why: Bowman draws sketches of the hibernating crew that HAL admires, and the final room is furnished with paintings, but no one is shown enjoying art.

fun-excitement.why: Poole plays chess with HAL, and Moon-Watcher, discovering the bone, smashes the tapir skeleton in a frenzy of play that becomes a weapon.

love-romantic.why: No romance; Poole's parents sing happy birthday by videophone and Floyd calls his daughter, but no lover appears.

love-family.why: Floyd calls his small daughter from the space station to ask what she wants for her birthday, and Poole's parents send a taped birthday greeting.

grief.why: Bowman silently retrieves Poole's body and then must let it go, and the apes huddle after the leopard takes one of them.

missing-someone.why: Floyd misses his daughter's birthday party, and Bowman is left with no one but HAL to talk to.

liking-as-a-friend.why: Bowman and Poole work as a quiet, trusting team, and HAL calls himself the sixth member of the crew before he kills four of them.

empathy.why: Bowman keeps pulling HAL's memory blocks while HAL pleads and sings, visibly affected, and HAL claims to sense Bowman's unease about the mission.

compassion.why: Bowman takes the pod out to recover Poole's body, and lets it go only when HAL forces him to.

grateful.why: Floyd thanks his hosts on the Moon; gratitude otherwise plays no part.

pleasure-from-helping.why: HAL says he enjoys working with people and puts himself to the fullest possible use, which is all any conscious entity can hope to do.

trustful-distrustful.why: Mission Control says HAL has made an error, Poole and Bowman hide in the pod to plan his disconnection, and HAL reads their lips; Floyd meanwhile feeds the Russians a cover story.

depressed.why: No one suffers a lack of support in a way the film dwells on; isolation is shown as calm, not despair.

angry.why: Moon-Watcher beats the rival ape to death at the waterhole, but HAL kills without anger and Bowman disconnects him in grim silence.

jealous-friendship.why: There is no friendship rank at stake.

hatred.why: The two ape tribes contest the waterhole until one is beaten with a bone, and HAL methodically kills the crew that would disconnect him.

contempt.why: HAL's calm refusal to open the pod bay doors has a note of condescension, but contempt is otherwise absent.

resentment.why: Moon-Watcher's tribe is driven from the waterhole by rivals and returns with the bone to take it back.

proud.why: HAL insists that the 9000 series has a perfect operational record and attributes the error to human error, and Moon-Watcher hurls the bone skyward in triumph.

amused.why: The zero-gravity toilet instructions and HAL's chess banter are jokes the characters barely notice.

sense-of-belonging.why: Two ape tribes face off at the waterhole, and Floyd fences politely with the Russian scientists about what the Americans are hiding at Clavius.

lonely.why: Bowman is left alone on Discovery after Poole dies and HAL is silenced, and ages alone in the white room at the end.

judgy-moral-sense.why: Bowman decides HAL must be disconnected after Poole's death, but the film offers little moral comment.

admiration.why: HAL admires Bowman's sketches; the apes stare at the monolith; nothing else earns regard.

embarrassed.why: Floyd squirms politely when the Russian scientist Smyslov presses him about the epidemic at Clavius.

guilt.why: HAL admits he has made some very poor decisions recently as Bowman pulls his memory, a flicker of something like guilt.

sad.why: HAL's slow dying, his mind going as he sings Daisy, and Bowman's silence afterward are the film's sadness.

happy.why: Floyd's cheerful call to his daughter and Poole's parents' birthday song are the film's only moments of ordinary happiness.

joyful-euphoric.why: Moon-Watcher's ecstasy as he smashes the skeleton and later hurls the bone into the sky is the film's one burst of triumph.

effort.why: Bowman forces his way into the ship through the emergency airlock and climbs into HAL's brain room to pull the memory blocks one by one.

focused-in-flow.why: Bowman and Poole go about the AE-35 replacement with absorbed precision, and Bowman works through HAL's disconnection step by step.

bored.why: Poole jogs the centrifuge and tans under a lamp, meals are routine, and the BBC interviewer asks how the crew copes with the monotony of the long voyage.

distracted.why: No one's attention wanders; the crew's routines are exact.

impatient.why: No one is in a hurry; the film's time is slow.

curious.why: The apes reach out to touch the monolith, Floyd's team photographs the one at Tycho, HAL asks about the mission's secrets, and Bowman flies his pod toward the monolith at Jupiter.

surprised.why: The Tycho team is caught off guard by the signal, Bowman is stunned when HAL refuses to open the doors, and he finds himself in a lit Louis XVI room beyond Jupiter.

awe.why: The apes gather in wonder around the monolith, Floyd's team stands before it on the Moon, and Bowman passes through the Star Gate into transformation.

skeptical-doubtful.why: Mission Control's twin 9000 contradicts HAL's fault report, Poole and Bowman come to doubt HAL, and the Russians openly doubt Floyd's epidemic story.

feeling-of-knowing.why: No one strains after a memory.

confused.why: Poole and Bowman cannot understand how a unit HAL called faulty tests perfect, and Bowman, aging in the white room, cannot understand where he is.

frustrated.why: Bowman repeats open the pod bay doors, HAL, to a machine that will not, and must find another way in through the emergency airlock.

uncertain-certain.why: Poole and Bowman weigh whether to disconnect HAL, and HAL, certain of his own perfection, decides the crew must go.

understanding.why: Moon-Watcher, after the monolith, grasps that the bone is a weapon, the film's central act of understanding, and Bowman becomes something that understands more than we see.

inspired.why: The monolith's touch gives Moon-Watcher the inspiration to pick up a bone as a club, and the match cut to the orbiting satellite makes that one insight the hinge of history.

satisfied.why: The apes retake the waterhole and Bowman silences HAL, but satisfaction is not a note the film lingers on.

foreboding.why: The apes huddle through uneasy nights, HAL's too-calm voice unsettles Bowman and Poole, and the monolith's silent presence fills everyone with a dread they cannot name.

nostalgia.why: HAL, dying, returns to the song Daisy that Mr Langley taught him when he was first activated.

anticipation-suspense.why: Bowman and Poole wait to see whether the AE-35 unit fails as HAL predicted, and Bowman waits in the pod for HAL to open the doors.

hope.why: Bowman hopes HAL will relent and let him in, and Floyd's mission hopes the monolith will answer.

elevation.why: Bowman's transformation into the Star Child is beyond any character's moral uplift; no one witnesses a good deed.

rage.why: Moon-Watcher's frenzied smashing and killing with the bone is rage discovered.
